entries.title: Withings BodyScan 2 Review: Worth Its Weight
entries.summary: After months of testing, this high-end smart scale has made me rethink how much a bathroom weigh-in can tell me.
entries.content:
I’m going to be honest from the start: No, you probably don’t need a $600 scale in your bathroom if you are just doing occasional weigh-ins. Hell, I don’t even know that elite athletes need to make this kind of extreme outlay even if they need to periodically check on how their training is going.

But I’m going to make the case for the Withings BodyScan 2 anyway. After spending several months with the device, the scale and its ecosystem have forced me to dig deeper into my health than ever before. At this point, I’m not sure I could go back to an older-model scale—even a very smart one like the original Withings Body Smart, which I used for years.

Getting a Handle on Health

There’s not much to distinguish the BodyScan 2 hardware from other smart scales aside from its handlebars, an indication that this device belongs to the now-burgeoning full-body scanner or body composition scale category. The device is, however, sleeker than most of its competition, featuring a svelte handle that somehow finds room for a small color LCD screen without the need for any extra bulk. All of your body metrics are showcased on this screen in real time, as they’re being measured, alongside any quick tips from Withings about how to get the best reading each time you hop on.

The unit offers two types of weigh-ins. Daily scans take about 30 seconds and include weight, an estimate of muscle and fat percentage (whole body and segmented across torso, arms, legs, and viscera), an estimate of basal metabolic rate, vascular age, and pulse wave velocity—though only a portion of these measurements are displayed live on the display.

entries.title: Omega Has New Bond Watches Even if There Isn’t a New James Bond
entries.summary: With no new 007 actor named and no film in the near future, Omega has had to get creative to keep its lucrative spy-watch train running.
entries.content:
It's been five years since James Bond was on the silver screen in No Time to Die. For fans of the secret agent, the wait has been arduous, made even harder by the fact that Amazon, which now owns the franchise, still hasn't chosen a successor to Daniel Craig, let alone started filming Bond's resurrection.

But if it's seemed like a long haul for fans, just think how it has felt for Omega, which counts on a steady stream of Bond action to regularly inject lots of lovely cash into the company via watch releases linked directly to the films. Omega's last official Bond film tie-in watch was the titanium No Time to Die Seamaster prematurely launched back in 2019, ahead of the film’s then Covid-delayed release in 2021.

Considering that Swatch Group’s net profit collapsed by almost 90 percent to $32 million in 2025 (though, thankfully, things look rosier so far this year), we shouldn't be surprised that Omega isn't bothering to wait for Jeff Bezos to put his white cat down and proceed with world domination. As there's no new Bond or Bond film to work with, Omega has decided to launch 007-themed watches anyway—not just one, but an entire collection totaling six Seamaster Divers.

You can hardly blame the brand. When Omega first strapped a Seamaster to Pierce Brosnan's wrist in 1995's GoldenEye, it reportedly saw a 20-fold sales increase. In 2012, Omega's then-president Stephen Urquhart even told Variety that Omega’s sales “look like a stock market chart” that peaks during promotion of Bond films, then sinks afterward. “The films have had a very marked influence on sales,” Urquhart conceded.

The new “James Bond and Spectre” collection is themed around good and evil, with three watches bearing the “007” symbol of James Bond, and three the octopus-like motif of Spectre, the fictional global terrorist organization in the series.

The six Seamaster Diver 300M watches share the same movement. However, the two non-limited stainless-steel editions are the core pieces, available individually at $8,600 each—one with a blue aluminum dial dedicated to James Bond, and the other black for dastardly Spectre fans. Both come on a brushed mesh bracelet.

The James Bond edition has a grade 5 titanium bezel, while the Spectre edition boasts a black ceramic bezel ring to match the dial's blackened grained finish.

The remaining four Seamasters are split across two limited-edition numbered sets—one dedicated to Bond, the other to Spectre—capped at 77 boxes each. At a cool $89,800 per pair (Omega won't sell them individually), you get one stainless-steel model on a brushed mesh bracelet, and a second in platinum-gold on leather.

Each set comes in a presentation box with an additional NATO strap, strap-changing tool, cuff links, a cord bracelet, a loupe, a leather travel pouch and card holder, and papers. In the James Bond set, the strap keepers are engraved with 007; in the Spectre set, the strap keepers carry the Spectre emblem.

This collection is not the first time Omega has sought to leverage its Bond connection without a film peg. Back in May of this year, Omega unveiled the Seamaster Diver 300M Chronograph “007 First Light,” a new 44-mm chrono tied to 007 First Light, a James Bond game developed by the same studio responsible for the Hitman franchise. Originally designed as an in-game gadget, Omega turned it into a production model.

Back in 2012, there was the Seamaster James Bond 007 50th Anniversary watch with a red number 50 on the bezel. In 2019, there was an On Her Majesty's Secret Service edition Seamaster to mark 50 years of the 1969 film, limited to 7,007 pieces. Then, in 2022, Omega released a Seamaster to coincide with 60 years of Bond movies.

entries.title: A Prediction Market About the Past? Sure, Why Not!
entries.summary: As prediction markets surge in popularity, a new platform called Verifact Markets is pushing the concept even further, letting users trade on “disputed facts.”
entries.content:
Would you put money on whether Covid-19 originated from a lab? How about whether some of the footage from the Apollo 11 moon landing was actually filmed on Earth?

Verifact Markets, a new startup that bills itself as a “prediction market for disputed facts,” is betting that people will be eager to weigh in on questions like these. The company’s premise is so quirky it sounds like something a couple of philosophy and economics majors dreamed after too many bong rips in their dorm room: Instead of wagering on the future, why not trade on stuff that already happened?

When Verifact Markets launched on Friday, some of the initial topics traders could take a position on included whether Jeffrey Epstein died by suicide and whether insurance behemoth State Farm “intentionally delayed” claims related to the 2025 Los Angeles wildfires. The featured market during beta testing was, indeed, about the origins of Covid-19. (As of writing, the market is still open, with “true” priced at 76 cents and “false” at 32; the majority of participants had put money on the pandemic beginning at Wuhan Institute of Virology.)

Verifact Markets is being funded and incubated by Positron Capital Management, the family office of tech investor Peter Wokwicz. He envisions the startup as a way to settle debates over hot-button issues like the amount of energy consumed by AI data centers. “I’m excited, because nobody’s done this before,” Wokwicz says. “We’re not going to shy away from controversial markets.”

In a regular prediction market, participants buy financial instruments known as event contracts, which are pegged to whether a specific event will take place in the future. Topics range from which team will win the Super Bowl to what the price of bitcoin will be in 15 minutes to whether the US and Iran will reach a nuclear deal. Someone who buys a “yes” contract on Polymarket that the Bears will start Case Keenum next week will make money if that happens. Similarly, someone who bets “no” on Kalshi that it will rain in Miami tomorrow will lose money if there’s a downpour.

Each prediction market has its own rules about how it resolves events, and sometimes things can get messy, like when Polymarket bettors tussled over whether Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelensky actually wore a suit, or when Kalshi traders revolted over how the platform settled a market on whether Iran’s supreme leader would leave power.

Verifact Markets’ setup is even messier. That’s by design, since the platform focuses specifically on scenarios where people disagree on what took place. It lists markets for past events that it considers “disputed” and lets its customers wager “true” or “false” on whether they really happened. People can also submit “evidence” for or against their position, and the company plans to offer rewards for credible documentation that helps resolve markets. If Verifact Markets determines that there’s enough evidence to make a call, it does so. If it still can’t tell, the company will “expire” a market and pay out users based on its calculation of the odds at the time.

According to Verifact Markets chief executive and cofounder Rodrigo Aquino, the markets themselves won’t determine whether something is true or false. That means even if all of the customers in a given market voted “true,” that won’t necessarily make it so. Trading prices will be factored in alongside other evidence and documentation that is submitted to the company by users. It is also planning to launch its own research system, which Aquino describes as “patent pending.” When I ask Aquino how the system works, he keeps the answer impressively vague: “We are analyzing, multi-dimensionally, a multitude of data points,” he says, noting that the process is “very mathematical, very quantitative” and also “very secretive.”

When I point out that credibly determining how the Covid pandemic started would be a massive news story, resolving a mystery that has eluded scientists for years, Aquino remains upbeat. “It’s doable,” he says.

Verifact says that it is currently in talks with market makers about providing liquidity. Right now, the project is so small that it is being bootstrapped by Positron Capital Management. There are a number of ongoing lawsuits in the US over whether prediction markets should be considered financial instruments or gambling, but it’s hard to discern how Verifact would factor into that debate because of its rather odd business model.

For the time being, the company is only offering its markets to people outside of the United States as it looks for the most viable legal path forward domestically, as it is not a licensed exchange in the US. But Wokwicz claims he purchased a regulated financial exchange in the last year and intends to roll Verifact into it when he can. Like Polymarket’s decentralized product, Verifact Markets is “on-chain,” and participants can make trades with stablecoins, a class of cryptocurrencies tied to the price of the US dollar and other fiat currencies.

Verifact Markets is part of a wave of startups interested in resolving the facts about disputed news and historical events. One of the most recent entries was the short-lived Peter Thiel–funded project Objection (later rebranded as The Primary), which aimed to determine whether specific media stories were accurate. But before the truth-adjudication stuff really got off the ground, The Primary pivoted to publishing news and a scoreboard for ranking journalists.

For now, there are very few details about how Verifact Markets will ultimately determine whether something is true or false, even though its entire value proposition rests on the idea that it’s uniquely positioned to do so. It's an extremely tall order, made even taller by all the other details that haven’t been worked out yet, like how the project will make money—it doesn’t plan to charge fees at launch. Wokwicz isn’t focused on that sort of thing, at least not yet. “What I'm looking forward to most is just some of the very unique evidence that people are going to dig up,” he says. “We're going to bring out truth—what is true and false.”

Some prediction market veterans say they are intrigued by Verifact Markets, even if there are plenty of remaining questions about how it will work. “I'll probably join just so I can keep making money off of the 2020 election for the rest of my existence,” says prominent prediction market trader Caleb Davies.

entries.title: Staples Print and Marketing Services Review: Fast Holiday Gifts
entries.summary: Staples’s printing service offers fast pickup and in-store experts who can help you get your family photos, novelty gifts, and business documents looking exactly how you want.
entries.content:
I print all the time, and not just because I test printers, but because I like paper. It doesn't matter if they're documents, photos, posters, or banners; I like artifacts—everything is better in physical form. And it's not just dinosaurs like me; while eschewing digital media, Gen Z is embracing printed matter, too (see, the kids are alright).

I've lost track of how many photo books I've printed over the years—mostly one-offs of little projects, fun things for friends, and maybe five copies at most. I'm not a photographer anymore, but old habits die hard, especially when you see the way people react to paper books. The response to a book, versus showing someone your latest Instagram post, is not even comparable.

With the holiday season kicking off, it seems apropos to point out that photo books make great gifts, as do mugs, prints, and my personal favorite for kids: photo puzzles. I've tested dozens of printing services over the years, and one of my favorites for holiday gifts is Staples.

You can order Staples prints online through the company's website, which features a variety of tools to help you design your photo gift, be it a mug, print, or puzzle. The print quality is great, and the online tools are well done and easy to use. But while ordering online is convenient, it's not why I like Staples for printing. It's because I can go to my local store and talk to actual human beings about my printing needs.

Printing can be tricky, and preparing your digital files exactly how the printer wants them isn't always easy. Best practice is to provide a high-res, flattened PDF file in CMYK color, but if you don't know what that means or how to get your file into the right format, fear not. The best way to print, even if you do know how to format it accurately, is to bring the file to your local Staples and talk to the print and marketing specialists there. They can catch potential issues before you print, and in most cases they can print a proof (sometimes at a reduced size, but still a proof) so you can see what you're getting beforehand. This is one advantage over online-only services.

Another big advantage is that you can get your gifts the same day if you pick up in-store. If you're in a rush this holiday season, remember that tip. You can even order online and pick up in-store to save yourself a trip, just be sure the place your order before noon.

Want to really step up your game? Here's my pro tip. Head to your local Staples to place your order, but have them print it at a Staples production center. Tell the store to have the production center send proofs for you to approve in person. This eliminates the same-day advantage, as it will likely take several days—sometimes as much as two weeks—but the printing quality will be better.

What's the quality like? I printed a couple of 11-ounce mugs—other options include a 15-ounce mug and a 17-ounce travel mug—and the results were on par with other services I've tested. I happen to like the shape of the Staples mugs a little more than what I got from others, but that's more personal preference than anything. For the design, you can choose a premade template and upload a photo of your choice, or you can start from scratch and design your own mug. As with all Staples printing services, you can choose same-day pickup if you want five or fewer. For larger orders, you'll need to get them delivered.

The photo options, like mounted prints, are nice. The print quality here lags behind dedicated photo services like our top picks, Mpix and Printique, but for the price it's quite good (both Mpix and Printique are more expensive). They offer canvas prints, metal prints, foam-backed prints, and posters up to 36 by 48 inches.

Staples is also a great place for business printing. I'm in the process of transitioning back to running a business, and the first thing I did wasn't setting up an Instagram account or doing anything with social media. The first thing I did was print business cards. Staples online business card maker is fantastic. And if I had a physical presence for my business, I'd have printed banners and posters and signs and everything else. Because we live in the real world, and if you want your business to succeed offline, you're going to need to print.

entries.title: 15 Best Office Chairs of 2026—We Tested 70 to Pick Them
entries.summary: Upgrade your WFH setup and work in style with these comfy, WIRED-tested seats.
entries.content:
Featured in this article

There Are Three things you don’t skimp on if you want a happy life: a good mattress, a good pair of shoes, and the best office chair you can find. Each is key to a world free of unnecessary pain. Finding the right ergonomic chair can be the difference between a satisfying and focused home office life and a squirmy day filled with cricks and small dissatisfactions.

The best desk chair is almost always an adjustable chair—one that can be tailored to your body’s unique shape and that offers enough lumbar support to avoid back problems even after long hours at the grind. Many chairs also utilize materials that can dissipate body heat, so you’re not stuck in Zoom meetings with a sweaty back. But the chair options out there can be bewildering. Luckily, the WIRED Reviews team has spent more than seven years sorting them out. WIRED Gear editor Julian Chokkattu has tested more than 60 chairs at his last tally. Reviewer Mathew Korfhage and other staffers have tried more than a dozen more, and most of our top picks have been tested by multiple people with different heights and body types.

WIRED’s favorite office chair for most people is the Branch Ergonomic Chair Pro ($499) because of its balance between value, features, comfort, and adjustability. That chair, and its lower-budget Ergonomic Chair ($369) cousin, have been tested and attested to by multiple WIRED reviewers. But we also offer chairs for every budget, from the preternaturally comfortable Steelcase Gesture ($1,510) to a $150 chair from Staples that leaves cheap Amazon brands in the dust.

We all have differing body types and needs, which is why we’ve put together a broad collection of recommendations—and why we enlist people of all sizes to keep testing our top picks for comfort and durability. Hopefully, we have a home office chair for you here.

For more home office buying guides, check out our Best Standing Desks, Best Laptop Stands, Best Home Office Gear, Best Mechanical Keyboards, and Best Webcams guides.

Updated October 2026: We tested the newly released Humanscale Freedom Ocean Headrest and added it as WIRED’s favorite reclining chair. We also added the Sihoo Doro S300 and Amseatac Crisscross Chair, streamlined our top picks, updated links and pricing throughout, and removed discontinued items.

Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.

How to Sit Properly at a Desk

The right chair can only go so far. Your sitting habits and posture matter too. We've rounded up several tips on how to set up your desk properly here, and how to avoid tech neck, but here are a few highlights.

Sitting for long stretches during a day is not good for your health, no matter what chair you use. It increases the risk of type 2 diabetes, stroke, and heart disease. The best thing you can do is get up and move every half hour. If you can, a 40-minute walk per day can, according to a recent study, make a big difference in countering some effects of a sedentary lifestyle. You probably don't need to bother with an active chair. Home office users should consider a standing desk that lets you swap between standing and sitting work positions during the day. A smartwatch can help too. Most have movement reminders that encourage you to stretch your legs. If you're dealing with back pain, consult your physician first.

Make sure your chair's armrests are adjustable. Your palms should be elevated over your desk, which should be at elbow level, and your wrists should be straight. If the bottom of your palm is resting on the desk or wrist rest, there's a chance you're putting too much pressure on your nerves, which could lead to issues like carpal tunnel syndrome. Talk to your physician if you're feeling any kind of pain. A gaming mouse, often more ergonomic than a standard mouse, might be helpful; just make sure to find one that fits your palm size.

When you look forward, your eyes should align with the top of your monitor or laptop. That might mean finding a chair that can adjust up and down, elevating your laptop with a stand, or raising the height of your monitor. This puts less pressure on your neck and spine—you shouldn't be craning your neck up or down.

What Should I Look for in an Office Chair?

A good rule of thumb is that the more adjustable a chair is, the better. This gives you the possibility to mold it to your body shape, which hopefully makes it a comfier and more supportive seat. Here's what you should be able to adjust on a chair.

Armrests: Most chairs let you move the armrests side to side, up and down, forward and back. It's even nicer when you're able to lock the armrest into place so that they don't slide around as your elbows rest on them. The armrest should naturally allow your palms to slightly hover over the desk. You'll often see descriptors like “4D” and “5D" adjustable armrests, which denote how many directions you can adjust them.

Seat height: It's worth checking a chair's maximum and minimum height before you buy because they might not work for your current desk (unless you have a standing desk where you can adjust the height). This is usually controlled with a pneumatic lift lever under the chair—pull the lever and get off the seat to let the chair go up, then sit on it and pull the lever to bring it down to your preference. Your feet should be planted on the floor at a 90- or 100-degree angle. If your chair arrives and it doesn't get as high as you'd like, don't worry, there's a very simple fix. Some office chair brands offer “tall cylinders" for not a lot of money, and if not, you can usually find third-party options on retailers like Amazon (make sure you buy for your specific chair!). Simply swap your existing cylinder with the tall version, and you'll have a greater height range to work with. You may be able to choose this option before checking out, or reach out to the company to see if they can swap it for you.

Seat depth: Seat depth is important for taller folks. There is usually a mechanism that lets you pull the seat out so that your thighs get the proper support. There should be one to two inches between the front of the seat and the back of your knees. Taller people with longer legs may not get the best support if they can't adjust the seat depth.

Seat tilt: This isn't as common as the above adjustments, but tilting the seat up or down may help posture and prevent back pain, though it can take some getting used to.

Lumbar support: Most office chairs offer lumbar support, which can look like a separate piece attached to the backrest that can slide up and down or back and forth. This piece supports your lower back (the lumbar region), specifically maintaining the curve of the spine to maintain good posture as you sit and, ideally, warding off back pain. Check your chair manufacturer's assembly instructions to learn how to adjust the lumbar support, and place the support on the curve of your lower back. What I like to do is run my hand along my spine until I reach the natural dip, then I try to make sure the lumbar support sits at that exact location. Some chairs also let you adjust the depth of the lumbar support, pushing it further inward or outward. Make sure it feels natural and that it's not digging in. Play around with this until it feels comfortable. Your shoulders should align with your hips, and you shouldn't feel like you're leaning forward.

Recline: Almost every office chair lets you lock or unlock the recline, but some go a step further and let you tweak the tension of the recline. This allows you to use more or less force when you lean back, which comes down to how much resistance you want when you lean back.

How We Test Office Chairs

Testing home office chairs is not for the minimalist. WIRED reviewer Matthew Korfhage and WIRED editor Julian Chokkattu—who's tested office chairs for seven years—might have four or five office chairs in their home at any given time. That's because office chairs take time to test. We sit in each for at least two weeks before we offer the barest opinion, because it takes time to gauge comfort. Some chairs take a moment to break in, and it can take even longer to gauge the supportiveness of each chair. Julian is 6' 4," and Matthew is 6' 1." But we solicit feedback from people of various heights while testing, including Julian's 5' 1" wife. Any chair that Matthew recommends but can't keep is used long-term by a durability tester, ideally a different height.

We try out all the adjustments throughout the testing period, both to see how the settings affect comfort, but also to check for tolerances and jiggle, which are red flags for durability: Seat adjustments, and armrest adjustments, are often the places where lesser chairs can fail first, long before the fabric starts to pill.

But it's not just about durability and lumbar support. These chairs will live in a home office for years, so aesthetics are important as well. We also research each chair company, looking into their warranties, customer service, customer feedback, reports to consumer agencies, and overall reliability. An office chair is meant to be a long-term investment. If a company can't stand behind its products, WIRED won't either.

How Does WIRED Select Chairs to Be Reviewed?

We routinely look at the market to find new office chairs that have hit the scene, whether it's from a newcomer or an established brand like Herman Miller. We check in on most chairs that someone credible has called their favorite, though we might not end up agreeing—and we're always on the lookout for chairs that fill a specific niche in the market. Julian and Matthew typically reach out to these companies to ask for the product, but do not promise any kind of editorial coverage—that goes against WIRED's editorial policies. Yes, WIRED earns affiliate revenue if you purchase an office chair using our link, but this is not factored into the decision-making process.

This said, we can't test every single chair that hits the market, in part because our testing regimen usually involves weeks of testing. And so you may indeed find some notable missing options in this guide, even after seven years of testing. We'll keep filling in the blanks on the top options in the market, and test new entrants.

After we've finished testing a chair, we either donate to Goodwill or keep it on hand for durability testing. Julian keeps top picks like the Branch Ergonomic Chair Pro, Herman Miller Embody, and Anthros V2 on hand to test against future contenders. Matthew does the same, but also places some chairs in the hands of durability testers of different heights, in order to see how they fare with different body types and how they hold up over time.

Does My Office Chair Need Lumbar Support?

In short, probably. If you sit in a chair all day, you likely want a chair with lumbar support.

We lead unnatural lives, evolutionarily speaking: The human body was not meant to sit for eight hours at a time in the same position. Unless you, blessed creature, have perfect posture—a difficult achievement when typing at a keyboard and looking at a monitor—the lower curve of your back might need a little extra support when sitting for long spans.

A relatively flat-backed or concave chair will often grant excellent support to your shoulders and back, but leave your lower back to fend for itself. Eventually, it complains.

“Your back has this natural curve to it, and if you're sitting in a chair that doesn't help support that natural S-curve, over time, it's going to feel a little bit less comfortable,” said Kristianne Egbert, an ergonomist at Briotix Health, in an interview with WIRED about lumbar support in late 2025. “When you're sitting in a forward, hunched position, and don't have that curve in your lower back, it increases the forces on the discs in your lower back, definitely resulting in discomfort.”

Experts are pretty univocal on the benefits of lumbar support. But not all lumbar support is created equal. Look for lumbar support that's adjustable, especially vertically so that the curve of the chair can line up with the curve of your back. Horizontal adjustability can adjust support to the level that's most comfortable for you. Cheaper chairs are less likely to offer adjustable support, and can instead make you feel like you're being pushed.

This said, if you can't afford a chair with excellent adjustable lumbar support, you're not doomed to a life of pain. A low-cost lumbar pillow like this one from LoveHome offers a workable fix.

Best Office Chairs for Specific Needs

Here are a few other chairs we recommend for specific needs and use cases.

Arguably, the smartest-designed reclining chair we've ever tested is the Humanscale Freedom, which we first wrote about more than 20 years ago and which still inspires lean-back bliss. The reason is the way the chair adjusts itself to the weight of your body, cradling your shape at any and all reclining positions without the need for fiddly levers. Designed by legendary designer Niels Diffrient, this chair combines lovely materials and colors, plush but firm support, adjustable seat height and depth, height-adjustable lumbar support, and a headrest that both fellow WIRED reviewer Julian Chokkattu and I heartily recommend. The recline system is fundamentally unique, with the back and lumbar moving semi-independently from the headrest to keep you facing forward, not at the ceiling. It takes getting used to, but is a nice perk if you're leaning back and looking at a screen. The Humanscale is also ecologically net-positive—think rainwater catchment systems, and materials designed from recycled fishnets—and also quite durable. The model Matthew tested, the Freedom Ocean, is made using recycled ocean fishnets in its headrest and reclining mechanism. The 15-year warranty is a nice assurance, as well.

The Vari is a much more affordable option that is also excellent for those prone to leaning back. The first time reviewer Matthew Korfhage leaned back all the way and closed his eyes while sitting on the Vari Align office chair (7/10, WIRED Recommends), he nearly conked out and missed an afternoon meeting. Despite its mesh-backed office-chair minimalism, this Align is somehow as comfortable as an old BarcaLounger when you dip it back. The reasons for this comfort are twofold. The first is the suspension system that maintains lower back support and stable balance while allowing a full 45-degree recline. The second is a cleverly designed mesh headrest that’s integrated into the chair back, forming a single sinuous curve that avoids hard edges. Like our top-pick Branch Ergonomic Pro, this Vari pairs a comfortable foam seat with the breathability and flexibility of a soft, non-abrasive mesh back. The Align is priced about as affordably, but does not offer quite the level of adjustability of the Branch. It might also be a bit too roomy or tall for those under 5' 6". The depth, but not the height, of the lumbar support can be adjusted. So can the seat depth and height, and pretty much everything about the arm position. Like all things Vari, the chair is among the easiest to assemble of any chairs we've tested, a five-minute job once you’re done unpacking.

Most ergonomic office chairs provide lumbar support to alleviate the ill effects of long-term sitting. These chairs have a different philosophy. They allow or even encourage you to move around a lot, thus avoiding the problems of sitting in one place for too long. Look for more info on these kinds of active chairs here. The consensus, after speaking with experts, is that you're better off getting a normal chair and introducing more movement into your workday, even if you're just standing up to get some water every hour. But if you need extra encouragement, these are the best options we've found.

The Ariel chair is designed to keep you moving. It's also the best active chair WIRED reviewer Julian Chokkattu found after testing several active chairs. The Ariel's shape targets the sitz bones in your pelvis to ensure you sit upright. Its base rocks around slightly, so your body will continually shift a little throughout the day. But also, the chair's generally aggressive form will cause you to get up more often, and move around more. There's a bit of a learning curve, noted WIRED gear team editor Julian Chokkattu, but over time he found himself with less back pain and better posture. The newer the Ariel 2.0 is pricier but has a comfier seat and more stability, even with the wheels add-on. For $100 less, the 1.0 remains a solid option but has lower weight capacity.

A crisscross chair is designed for those for whom armrests are often the enemy: knee tuckers, crisscross sitters, stretchers, squirmers, fidgeters, and yoga practitioners. The idea is simple, allowing the armrests to fold down and be sat upon. The viral Pipersong Meditation Chair is the most famous of these, but we found the stool and chair back too small to be comfortable. WIRED contributing reviewer Nicole Kinning found this Amseatac Crisscross Chair (8/10, WIRED Recommends) to be wider, cushier, and more affordable.

The Zeph from Herman Miller is a unicorn, mixing minimalist, mid-century modern stylings with the ergonomic considerations of a modern office chair. It hearkens to a classic Saarinen tulip, with two-tone seat pads and dozens of fetching color options. But unlike most office chairs, adjustments are nearly nil, making this more of a task chair and lovely statement piece, but with surprising comfort. The Zeph is meant to mold around your body, and mostly succeeds in doing so. It's a great compact chair for smaller spaces, as well, and the 12-year warranty is a boon.

LiberNovo is a relatively new and mostly untested Hong Kong brand, and its chairs are quite literally humming with new ideas. The flashiest thing about the LiberNovo Omni Pro, released in July as the upgrade to last year's LiberNovo Omni (7/10, WIRED Recommends), is the battery-powered motor that repositions the lumbar support—avoiding cumbersome fiddling with adjustments behind the chair back. This battery also runs a nifty little fan below the seat to draw away heat from the chair's cushy foam. It even has a little spinal stretching massage function that's mostly a novelty. These features are attention-getting, but also lead to worries about longevity if the motor fails.

Gaming chairs must lean back well. They must be comfy for long hours of intense focus. And they must feel like something meant for play, not work. For more context and options, check in on WIRED's full gaming chair guide. But here are a couple standouts.

Maybe it should come as no surprise, but the gaming version of WIRED's favorite office chair is also WIRED's favorite gaming chair. As with the main Branch Ergonomic Chair Pro, assembly is a breeze, the price is approachable, and the chair is both sturdy and wonderfully adjustable across a broad range of heights. The “gaming” element is mostly aesthetic, offering any of three Sega-branded styles that include a mesh-backed blue Sonic chair that offers the same breathability as the original. But if you're into leather, gaming chair reviewer Louryn Strampe found that the Dreamcast and Genesis-colorway leather-backed chairs were not sweaty when leaning back and locking in for a long gaming session. Just note that if you're 5' 1" like she is, you won't get much use out of the headrest.

The Razer Iskur V2 NewGen does a solid job of mixing the typical flashy gaming chair design with something that doesn’t scream “Discord moderator.” In my few months with the chair, tester Louryn Strampe grew to really appreciate its mix of comfort and aesthetics—with adaptive lumbar support, 4D armrests, wide shoulders and a comfy seat. It's designed to stay a bit cooler than its predecessor, and remains accommodating even to cross-legged sitting. Strampe says she has successfully sat in this chair for literally 36 hours over a two-day stretch during a particularly intense Slay the Spire 2 marathon. (Judgment-free space, people.)

Office Chair Accessories

The wheels on the bottom of your chair are among the easiest parts to replace. If your current casters don't roll smoothly or are too loud, it might be worth replacing them instead of buying a whole new chair. These from Stealtho, a Ukrainian company, are a good pick tested by WIRED reviewer Julian Chokkattu. They'll work with nearly every office chair, though the company notes they don't fit Ikea products. The soft polyurethane material means these won't scratch or chip hardwood floors, as some plastic casters do, plus it'll feel like you're silently gliding as you roll from your desk to the fridge (don't judge).

Fair warning: Since these are more frictionless than normal casters, they can cause your chair to roll around sometimes, like when you stand up and walk away. Stealtho has locking casters if you're worried about your chair rolling, and they don't cost much more (these weren’t in stock last time we checked).

Do you need a mat for your chair? Probably not. However, casters can scuff up hard floors, which is why we recommend upgrading them to rollerblade wheels (see above). If you're on a carpet, it can also be hard to move around. A mat can help with both of these issues. WIRED senior gear editor Julian Chokkattu used this glass one from Vitrazza for two years and was pleasantly surprised. (You can go for much cheaper mats made from other materials, too.) The safety glass is thick, and Julian did not see any notable scratches even after that time. It holds 1,000 pounds and doesn't touch your hardwood floor, as you need to affix rubber bumpers to keep them apart. You can choose from several sizes, and Vitrazza sells various shapes too. It's just a bit difficult to clean since you have to lift it to get to all the dirt underneath.

If you can't upgrade your seat just yet, a cushion or backrest might help. Here are a few we like:

Cushion Lab Seat Cushion for $75 : This memory foam seat is comfortable, and I had no problems sitting on it for hours on end. It's best paired with an adjustable chair, as it adds a decent amount of height to your seat, which might make typing on a keyboard awkward. It does a great job of keeping out bad odors, and you can also wash the cover.

LoveHome Memory Foam Lumbar Support for $23: If you slouch in your seat, this comfortable memory foam pillow can help. It keeps your back straight and supported, and it's an affordable fix to try before shelling out hundreds for a new chair. It's good to use in a car or wheelchair, too. The cover is washable, and it has two adjustable straps (plus an extension strap) that go around your seat to keep it in position.

Secretlab Premium Footrest for $89: Ideally, your feet are planted on the ground as you sit, but it's nice to be able to prop them up on something soft every so often. I have tried a handful of footrests, and Secretlab's Premium Footrest is easily the best—I have been using mine for more than three years. Not only is the PlushCell memory foam material soft and cushy, but it also stays remarkably clean. I have a tiny dog, and his hair gets everywhere except the quilted fabric cover. (You can handwash this cover to get dirt out.) The patterned silicone base does a good job of keeping it in place, too.

More Office Chairs WIRED Recommends

Uplift Desk Intuition Ergonomic Chair With Headrest for $649: At a slightly higher price point, the ergonomically designed, breathable-mesh Intuition was a strong contender for favorite reclining chair. It's also a strong contender in general, and the chair back's three overlapping mesh panels make it distinctly techy-looking. Like WIRED's favorite affordable recliner, the lower-cost Vari Align, the Intuition allows you to halt the recline anywhere along the path from 90 to 45 degrees—with an added tension control knob to adjust the speed and ease of your descent. The height of the lumbar support is adjustable up and down, and otherwise tilts and flexes to meet your back. The headrest is adjustable by both height and angle, and can also be removed entirely. But note that while the curved lower section of the chair's back offers strong lumbar support, it's also pretty aggressive and takes some getting used to. So is the durable nylon mesh, which will feel scratchy in your summer clothes, especially as you're reclining. But the strong ergonomic support will be a big sell for many, especially with the chair's near-infinite adjustability. Just note that taller people might not find that the armrests or the seat go high enough. At 6'1", tester Matthew Korfhage felt he was right on the edge. Construction is solid, with mostly chrome and aluminum on the lower frame. The warranty is a lovely 15 years.

Uplift Desk Clarksville Ergonomic Chair for $399: The Clarksville is a mid-budget chair model from Uplift. It's a type of chair I generally quite like: breathable, soft-fabric mesh back and a comfortable foam bottom, which tends to settle in over the course of a couple weeks. The overall look is boxy, utilitarian, and respectable. Like the Intuition from Uplift, the chair offers deep reclining ability that can be halted anywhere en route to 45 degrees. But the suspension doesn't offer quite the same level of lumbar support on the way down, nor is there a headrest. Which is to say the Clarksville is best at merely a slight leanback, versus a deep recline. But in the end, the Clarksville is the sort of chair you won't think about much after you buy it, which in its own way is a virtue. A 15-year warranty on a chair below $400 makes this even more virtuous.

Haworth Zody Bouclé Office Chair for $1,610: Haworth's Zody is an attractive and elegant chair, especially in the bouclé version Julian Chokkattu tried. His test unit sadly didn't come with a lumbar adjustment, but he still felt quite comfortable sitting in it for long hours. It does run a little warm with this material, though the same will be true if you opt for leather or upholstered. (If that's an issue, you can also go with the standard mesh Zody for around $300 less.) It's very easy to lightly recline in it, and you can even tilt the chair into a more forward sitting position if you're doing a more active task. Julian didn't care much for the seat arms—they felt a little rattly—but found little else to complain about the chair. You get a 12-year warranty, and you can try it for 30 days to see if it's for you.

ProtoArc Flexer Pro for $167: This is a surprisingly decent office chair for the money. There are several adjustable points, including seat pan depth and four-way adjustable armrests, as well as multiple recline angles. The build quality is solid considering the price, and it looks nice. After two weeks of sitting on it, it feels relatively supportive, though the seat foam is a bit too firm, noted tester Julian Chokkattu. The main issue is that the lumbar support pops off the chair way too easily when he shifted in his seat. (It has happened three times now.) He wished it were integrated with the backrest.

Hon Nucleus Drafting Chair for $605: A drafting chair is designed to accommodate high work surfaces, and you'll usually see a ring underneath the seat to rest your feet on if they don't hit the floor. I'll admit I haven't tested many drafting chairs, but I found the Nucleus completely fine. It looks a bit dull, but the seat is medium firm, there's adjustable lumbar support, and the arms can move up or down and in or out. The version of the chair I tried did not have a recline function, but I was able to adjust the seat depth and seat height. I didn't find it offensive after several weeks of testing, but I also didn't fall in love. I don't think it's worth the MSRP. I also tried the standard Nucleus chair, which is available for a slightly lower price. This one did have the Synchro-Tilt mechanism, and it was easy to set the recline and lock it into place. It does the job, but I think Branch's Ergonomic Chair Pro is still the better buy.

Hon Altern Chair for $332: It's hard to find a good office chair in this price range. Most people will be better served with the Branch Ergonomic Chair pick above, which has dipped close to $300 during sale events, but the Hon Altern is a decent alternative. The best part about it is that the seat is wide and soft, so your butt will feel fairly comfortable, and the seat depth adjustment accommodates a larger group of people. However, the back support is lackluster. I want to be more upright, but the chair forces me to lean backward. The armrests can only move up and down—I wish I could move them inward a bit more. Its design is also generic. Still, I sat on the Altern for a month, and it does the job. If your budget is tight, it's far and away better than many of the options you'll find at this price on Amazon. It includes a headrest, too, which is typically an extra add-on for many chairs.

Autonomous ErgoChair Ultra 2 for $449: Julian Chokkattu sat on Autonomous’s 3D-printed ErgoChair Ultra 2 for over a month and was pleasantly surprised. It’s a big improvement over the original Chair Ultra, which had a flat and hard seat. The Ultra V2’s seat is still not as cushy as some chairs, but it doesn't feel like sitting on concrete. It has all of the adjustments you’d want, from seat depth to a recline lock, and Chokkattu didn't encounter any back pain. The all-mesh design offered good airflow, and the backrest was wide enough that it didn't dig into his shoulders. The only flaw? Sometimes when he put too much pressure on the armrest (like when getting up or shifting his weight), it moved down with a loud crack despite being locked in place. Also, Autonomous has a pretty lackluster two-year warranty despite the high price, and its customer service doesn't seem to be great. A reader provided feedback of a poor experience with the company, and that seems to track with other reports around the web.

Haworth Fern for $1,330: I think the Haworth Fern is best for shorter people (aka anyone not above 6 feet, like me). It's adjustable to the nth degree—you can even tilt the seat for a more upright sitting position—but the seat itself was just wide enough for me, though it's plenty soft and pillowy. When I pulled out the seat depth to the max, it created a gap between the seat and the backrest, and I didn't love this feeling. The backrest is nice and soft, but I'd argue the lumbar support is quite aggressive. My back just felt like something was there all the time, and it felt distracting. I don't think you'd have these issues if you were shorter and narrower, and it's otherwise one of the softest office chairs I've sat on.

Autonomous ErgoChair Pro for $499: Our top pick, the Branch Ergonomic Chair Pro, is a better buy, but if you need a headrest and want a wider seat, consider the Autonomous ErgoChair Pro. I sat on it for a month with no major problems, except that the box it came in was massive and barely fit through my front door. The levers also aren't super intuitive—I highly recommend checking out this video from the company when you first set it up to dial in your preferences. All the standard adjustments are present, from seat depth and lumbar support to fine-tuning the recline. What surprised me most was the ability to tilt the seat so it's angled down—you don't see that in many chairs. The overall build quality is solid, and I even enjoyed the headrest when kicking back to watch House reruns during lunch. The only woes? I wish the arms stayed locked, as they can slide back and forth. While the foam seat is quite comfy, it can get warm in a toasty room (though the mesh back helps keep things cool). It's a shame this company has an abysmal warranty period, and see my note above on its customer service record.

Staples Hyken for $300: The humble Hyken is frequently available for around $150 during big sale events, making it one of the most affordable good chairs out there. It reclines, has a breathable mesh fabric on the back and seat, and it's sturdy. You even get a headrest and lumbar support. After five years of continuous sitting, WIRED reviewers say the Hyken's mesh has compressed a bit, but it's still comfy. The Staples Dexley is slightly wider, so get it if you need a wider seat.

Nouhaus Ergo3D for $330: This is another all-mesh chair. The ElastoMesh seat isn't as comfy as the Steelcase Karman (it'll feel worse on the skin if you, uh, tend to sit at your desk without pants), but it's otherwise quite adjustable and roomy, plus it even comes with two sets of wheels (casters or rollerblades) so you can choose which works best for you and your flooring. If you're in a particularly hot environment, it won't trap heat and will keep your whole body cool for a fraction of the price of the Karman.

Haworth Breck for $435: Haworth's Breck office chair is likely best-suited for shorter people (roughly under 5'8"), though 6'4" tester Julian Chokkattu experienced no back pain when sitting in it for a month. That's because the Breck's seat is short, and the seat depth only extends an extra 2 inches. The weight-activated recline also requires some push on your end, more than you might expect—it wasn't too difficult, but lighter-weight people may find it problematic. The seat padding is thin, though this caused no issues even after hours of sitting. The best part is how amazingly simple it is to set up—no tools required! But the main gripe? Simply getting up from the seat causes the gas spring cylinder to loudly lift. This, and the fact that it tends to make some noises when one fidgets around, makes it feel a little cheap.

Branch Verve for $599: The Verve used to be a top pick, but the Ergonomic Chair Pro is likely a better value considering they're similar in price. It is elegant (especially in the lovely Coral and Cobalt colors), it keeps your back straight, and tester Julian Chokkattu found it quite comfy. It can make nearly the same adjustments as our top pick, but there's no seat tilt, and the armrests are much more limited. Taller or bigger people would probably prefer if the seat were a smidge wider. Note also that a colleague who owns the Verve has said that after more than two years, the seat started to sink whenever he sat on it. Thankfully, he says, Branch's customer service was very responsive and promptly sent him a new cylinder.

Eureka Ergonomic Royal Chair for $449: Some folks chase that executive aesthetic—you know, plush leather and a high back so you can swivel around and reveal a cat in your lap as you laugh maniacally? This chair from Eureka fits the bill without costing a fortune, and it was an OK chair for the month Julian Chokkattu sat in it. The setup was quick, and the seat and back are soft and a little bouncy. He nonetheless found his back sweaty after a few hours of sitting because there was just nowhere for body heat to go. The lumbar support isn't great, and prolonged sitting left Julian with some sensations in his lower back. Not pain, just his back telling him he ought to get up. There's not much to adjust, but the recline and headrest. Also, if you need a wide seat, this is not the chair for you, as the armrests will feel like they're boxing you in (it just fits Julian, who is 6'4"). The chair is easy to clean with a damp cloth, and the fake leather has held up. Too bad about the two-year warranty.

Secretlab Titan Evo for $579: The Secretlab Titan Evo is unique among gaming chairs in that it's classy enough for the home office. It sets itself apart from similarly priced competitors with its durability and flexibility. It’s comfortable for marathon gaming sessions, thanks to the adjustability it offers (particularly the lumbar support). The headrest pillow is magnetic and stays attached to the chair, which is a nice touch. But the firm, cold-cure foam molds to your body and may not suit everyone. It will also make you feel sweaty.

Hinomi X1 for $899: Hinomi's X1 mesh chair has a trick up its sleeve—a built-in footrest! Just extend and flip out the footrest; voilà, your feet are now propped up. This might not be very practical for tall people whose legs hit the wall behind their desks, but it's quite comfy. Tester Julian Chokkattu found the chair well-built, but said he didn't end up using the footrest as much as he thought he would. There are a good number of adjustments, and the seat itself is a bit firm, which Julian got used to after some time. Hinomi offers a 10-year warranty.

OdinLake Ergo Max747 for $899: The Ergo Max747 is, all around, a great seat to sit in. The three-piece back provides great support and comfort, and the easy-access paddles on either side of the seat make most adjustments quick and simple. Even sitting for hours, I never felt uncomfortable, whether I was sitting up or reclining (this chair reclines incredibly far, from 90 to 135 degrees). The bag holder in the back (which I typically used to hold a hat or small backpack) was a surprisingly nice touch, and the mesh backing and seat are breathable, preventing overheating during prolonged use. I still don’t know how I feel about the polished metal frame, and the inclusion of gloves for assembly makes me worry about how easily this seat will pick up smudges over the years, but the polished finish itself is spotless and well-executed. At 6' 3", I had to max out the back height to comfortably sit in the chair. The secondary adjustments (back height, lumbar support, and headrest height) were awkward to adjust due to complicated ratcheting mechanisms keeping them in place. However, the comfort and breathability of this chair make it a compelling choice. —Henri Robbins

Vari Task Chair for $429: Vari’s Task Chair is surprisingly comfy given its relatively simple construction. Former WIRED reviewer Medea Giordano tested it and asked her husband to use it during his long gaming sessions. They agreed that the angled back provides ample lumbar support to make those sessions comfortable. It also takes very little time to construct. You can recline a bit, but even at the lowest tension, it pushes you back up, and there’s no head support. It’s more for rocking than actually leaning. Her biggest gripe is that the armrests are quite hard. A little more padding would be a huge improvement.

Branch Softside for $299: Julian Chokkattu tested the high-back version of the Softside and liked it a lot. It's different from all the other chairs in this guide, a bit comfy and cushiony. If you need a wider seat, this might not be the option for you, as the armrests do box you in. There's not much to adjust, but Julian's back didn't have any issues after weeks of sitting for full workdays. The build quality overall is OK. Considering it starts at $299, the overall seating experience, and the lovely design in fun colors, this is a pretty good value if you are after a deep-cushioned experience.

BodyBilt Midcelli for $1,021: BodyBilt’s chair looks quite average, but the seat pad is plush and soft, and it contours to your butt and legs, which tester Julian Chokkattu liked more than he expected. The mesh back has some give to it, so it doesn't feel rigid, and there are all the usual points of adjustment, including moving the seat forward and back. I wish the arms could lock in position, though. It has a lifetime warranty on select parts, while other chair areas are covered for three to 12 years. There are more customization options on BodyBilt's website—with the option to get a consultation. These are all nice sells. But it's a hefty price compared to some of our top picks.

Tempur-Pedic Tempur-Lumbar Support Office Chair for $352: This is a nice alternative to the Branch Ergonomic Chair and the Tempur seat cushion is, perhaps unsurprisingly, wonderfully comfy to sit on for hours at a time. Most chairs that have a thick lumbar cushion end up causing me back pain, but not here—tester Julian Chokkattu had no issues sitting on it for a month. The mesh back is nice for airflow, too. The arms tend to move around a bit, though, and the mechanism to adjust them is not elegant. Installation wasn't too hard, but the instructions weren't as simple as Branch's, and the overall build quality feels cheap.

Etta Avenue Doreen Velvet Task Chair for $260: There's absolutely nothing you can adjust on this chair except its height, but it's cute, and the seat is comfy. The velvet polyester was surprisingly durable and looked nice even after several weeks of sitting on this chair. The gold finish on the frame and legs chipped off in one area when tester Julian Chokkattu was unboxing it—it's frequently under $200, OK? But the biggest issue is that it is not compatible with tall or larger people. Julian's wide shoulders caused his arms to stick out of this chair, making it difficult to type, but it suited his 5' 1" wife's narrower frame well. With a 30-day warranty, you get what you pay for, but this chair is more about aesthetics than anything else.

X-Chair X2 K-Sport Management Chair for $879: This used to be our top mesh chair pick, but it has been supplanted by the Steelcase Karman. Sitting in the X-Chair feels like lounging in a hammock. Every part of the body feels well supported, and you can adjust nearly everything on the chair. Pull the seat up and push the armrests up, down, and side to side, or angle them in or out. The lumbar support feels like a cushion, and it adjusts as you move in your seat. If you want to rest your head, you can pay extra for the headrest. It has held up extremely well after three years of near-continuous sitting, but it's also a bit bulky. X-Chair has several models to choose from. I tested the X-2 K-Sport with the wide seat, and it fits tester Julian Chokkattu's 6'4" frame well, but it was too wide for his partner, who is 5' 1". Most people should be fine with the standard X1.

X-Chair X-Tech Executive Chair for $1,845: Functionally, the X-Tech is similar to the X-Chair above. In this version, the M-Foam cooling gel seat is indeed wonderful to sit on, though it's not as heat-wicking as the all-mesh versions. It’s the Brisa Soft Touch material that's most impressive—it’s ridiculously soft. Stick with the standard armrests instead of the FS 360 armrests, which tend to move about too much. I just can't figure out why on earth it costs this much.

Mavix M7 for $777: If this looks strangely similar to the X-Chair (see above), that's because both are owned by the same company. The M7 has similarly adjustable armrests and seat angles, but you get wheels that lock. The mesh back and wide seat construction keep you cool and comfortable during sweaty League of Legends sessions, and the lumbar support does the job. WIRED gaming chair reviewer Louryn Strampe ran into some issues with assembly, but customer service was able to exchange the model without much effort. If you're short, contact customer support while ordering—Mavix offers shorter cylinders so your feet can touch the ground.

Ikea Markus for $250: The Markus is a perfectly fine office chair. It’s not the most comfortable, but it’s far from the worst. The mesh design keeps you cool, and the tall back lets you fully lean into it. It’s rather thin and isn’t obtrusive in a small home office or bedroom. It was annoying to put together (see: Ikea), and you might need someone to hold up the back of the chair while you properly attach the seat. Unfortunately, if you often sit with at least one leg up or with your legs crossed, the width between the arms will make you uncomfortable.

Hon Ignition 2.0 for $481: The Ignition 2.0 is easy to set up and looks great, but it's had mixed results among WIRED testers, despite positive reviews around the web. 6' 4" tester Julian Chokkattu experienced some back pain, but a 5' 4" friend tried it for a few weeks, and she had zero issues. This seems to be the answer. It's possible the Ignition is just better suited for smaller folks.

Pipersong Meditation Chair for $299: Have a problem sitting in a traditional chair? If your legs need to be bent and twisted for you to be comfortable, you'll want to check this seat out. It has a 360-degree swiveling footstool that can accommodate pretty much any sitting position you want. I can go from kneeling to cross-legged to one leg up, one leg down. It’s possible to sit normally too, with the footstool behind you and your feet flat on the floor. It's the most prominent chair designed for odd sitting habits. There are no armrests, which I didn’t mind because that’s what makes it possible to sit in many of these positions. The actual stool and chair back could stand to be bigger and taller, respectively. I had to use a pillow to keep my back comfy. —Medea Giordano

Avoid These Chairs

If you come across these models, we recommend you save your cash and go for one of the picks above.

Sihoo Doro S300 Pro V2: The update to the Doro S300 is priced more approachably than the original chair at under $500—a bit of a rarity for chairs marked as the “Pro” edition. Like the original, the Doro looks like a Space Age command chair built from a layer cake of shaped mesh panels. Its back is quite comfortable, with lumbar support that can be adjusted both inward and up and down. Like all mesh, it's quite breathable, and the chair is built to allow a lot of lateral movement, aligning with your body as you move side to side. This is all nice. But the chair's a bit squeaky, and its noodly, 8D-adjustable armrests are a bit of a deal-breaker for me. On the one hand, the armrests are shockingly adjustable, to seemingly any position. On the other, they move seemingly everywhere except where you want them, pushing out or tilting at the lightest touch, which can give the chair an oddly flimsy feeling. Also, the recline function is precipitous and unbalanced: I actually yelped in fear when leaning back for the first time, which bounced the chair slightly off its front wheels. Assembly takes more than an hour and involves 17 parts and 30 ill-labeled screws.

Eureka Ergonomic Serene Nox: This chair is easy to set up; however, after tester Julian Chokkattu sat on it for more than a week, two of the screws at the bottom of the frame came undone, and the left half of the seat suddenly dropped low. That's not something you should deal with for an $800 chair, and even after he tightened the screws, it happened again a few days later. It's a shame, because it's a fairly attractive leather office chair with a nice silhouette, and it's decently comfy. The construction just needs work.

Razer Iskur V2 X: Multiple WIRED reviewers recommend Razer's Iskur V2 Pro as the best gaming chair if you're after the racing car seat aesthetic, but the cheaper V2 X isn't as impressive. It's dramatically cheaper, but it's worth keeping in mind that the Iskur V2 has dipped to $400 during major sale events, so the V2 X isn't that much more affordable. The seat is actually OK; the built-in lumbar support helped keep back pain away even after long hours at the computer. The fabric upholstery keeps your body warm (and a little sweaty), but it's comfy to sit on. But the biggest issue for tester Julian Chokkattu? It creaked so dang much. After just a week or so of sitting on the V2 X, almost every part of the chair started creaking. You're going to have to WD-40 this thing every few weeks to keep it quiet. Or save your cash and go for the V2.

TopJob Napa: The Napa should be $200 or $250 at best, notes tester Julian Chokkattu, nowhere near its $450 to $550 asking price. It's not comfy, he notes, there's not much plush to the seat and backrest, but it's not too uncomfortable. Julian's back surprisingly didn't complain after more than a week of sitting in it for several hours a day. It doesn't have many points of adjustment—you can adjust the armrest height, lock the recline at a few degrees, and adjust tilt tension. That's it. Technically, you can adjust the headrest, but mine would not stay put at a specific height. You can pull out a footrest, but in practice this is more gimmicky than useful. It looks attractive, especially in the amber vegan leather, but the overall quality is a little cheap. You can do better at this price.

Humanscale World One: Despite hailing from the well-renowned Humanscale, this chair looks quite bland, noted tester Julian Chokkattu. The setup was fairly quick, and … interesting. You have to hammer two pegs to affix the backrest to the seat, which I've never had to do before, after testing dozens of office chairs. It just feels cheap and a little too plasticky. Like other Humanscale offerings, there are no adjustments to make as the chair will handle it all for you (you can adjust the seat and armrest height). Julian loved this on the pricier Humanscale Freedom, which felt like someone was cradling his body. But in the all-mesh World One, he found his body constantly shifting, trying to find a comfy way to recline. The mesh material also feels like it digs in a bit. This could all be because he's 6' 4", as the chair feels like it's better suited for less lofty people. But at $700, it's worth demanding more.

Herman Miller Vantum: Initially, tester Julian Chokkattu liked the Vantum. He liked how it could keep him in a super upright position, which made him feel more engaged in what he was doing. The mesh backrest also disperses heat quite well. However, the overall build quality feels cheap and doesn’t scream Herman Miller (nor does the asking price, which has since dropped just below four figures). The headrest isn't great either—Julian nearly broke it trying to move it up and down. As he kept sitting, it was the back support that disappointed him the most. You can feel the lumbar support on your lower back, and not in a good way, almost like it’s digging in. At least it didn’t cause back pain.

Vilno Nobel Kneeling Chair: This kneeling chair is what's known as an active chair, meant to keep your body moving and keep your posture straight. It was easy to put all the wood pieces together, and the seat cushion was surprisingly plump. It feels effective for the first few hours, but unfortunately, rocking in the seat tends to cause it to move around on the floor, so I frequently had to fix my position. Worse yet, my shins and knees grew fatigued, and I started feeling some pain after a few days. You can't adjust its height, so it needs to be paired with a standing desk so that your palms don't rest on your desk. —Julian Chokkattu

Flexispot C7: While this chair is simple to assemble and looks good, it feels flimsy. The entire back flexes and warps whenever you move, and the lumbar support is barely connected to the rest of the chair, meaning it audibly scratches against the main section of the back every time you adjust and hardly feels like it provides any actual support. The footrest bends whenever weight is put on it, and the foam seat cushion collects crazy amounts of pet hair. It feels like just a few extra screws and supports would have made this a good product, but in its current state, there isn’t enough material to make it feel sturdy. —Henri Robbins

Steelcase Series 1: WIRED reviewer Louryn Strampe says her biggest issue with the Series 1 is with the armrests—the tops slide back and forth and side to side, which could be a good thing, except she managed to pinch her arm every time she moved. There's no way to lock them in place, so while she felt supported, her arms weren't. The seat is also pretty curved, which can feel like you're trapped in one position as you work throughout the day.

Sihoo Doro S300: Former WIRED reviewer Medea Giordano tested the Doro S300, which, in white, looks like it came straight out of the Space Force situation room. She found it comfortable. There are several adjustments you can personalize, like seat depth and recline angle. You can recline quite far, but she says she wishes there were a footrest to enjoy the lowest recline position. She typically prefers a cushy gaming chair, but she says she had no trouble sitting on this seat all day—the dual lumbar support helps too. However, the headrest is too low for her to lean against, even at its maximum height, and the arms move too easily. Simply placing her arms down pushes them out of position. It's also squeaky and overpriced.
